title: ThinK: Explorative Modeling for Fine-Grained Geometry Estimation, from Regression to Flow Matching
teaser: Thin structures come out bent in feed-forward geometry estimation because a pointwise loss must predict the mean of two competing surfaces. This project adds best-of-K exploration (Explorative Modeling) to both ends of the objective spectrum — a one-pass latent-conditioned regression head and a few-step flow-matching depth model — asking how much generation factoring fine-grained geometry still needs once the training objective can commit to modes instead of averaging them.
abstract: Feed-forward geometry estimators such as MoGe and Depth Anything 3 recover global structure remarkably well, yet their local geometry fails in a characteristic way: thin structures — streetlamps, chair legs, railings — emerge bent or oscillatory in 3D, with distortion growing as the structure gets thinner and the background more distant (SurGe). Through the lens of generative expressivity this is an objective problem, not only an architecture problem: around a thin structure the per-pixel conditional p(depth | image) is bimodal (foreground or background), and a deterministic regressor trained with a pointwise loss must predict the conditional mean — a point floating between the two surfaces that no real scene contains. PointDiT showed one escape: swapping regression for generative flow matching lifts boundary F1 from 10.9 to 13.9 on the same architecture, at the price of multi-step sampling machinery. Explorative Modeling (XM) offers another: draw K candidate predictions per training step and backpropagate only the best-matching one, which provably turns the loss minimizer from the mean into committed modes (best-of-K squared error is a K-means-style quantization of the conditional) — and it applies to both objectives. This project studies XM across the full spectrum. Arm A (end-to-end XM on regression): a lightweight latent-conditioned refinement head on a frozen backbone, trained with best-of-K selection under an edge-sensitive scoring loss (point gradient matching), keeping inference a single forward pass; K=1 is the exact regression baseline. Arm B (hybrid XM on flow matching): fine-tune a released pixel-space few-step depth model (Pixel-Perfect Depth) with exploration over its input noise — same data sample and timestep, K noise draws, train the best coupling — leaving the sampler untouched. Hypotheses: (i) in both arms, boundary F1 and point-map normal error improve monotonically with K while AbsRel/delta1 stay flat; (ii) the failure mode transforms from off-manifold averaging (bent poles) to on-manifold commitment (straight, possibly sub-pixel-shifted poles); (iii) exploration substitutes for generation factoring — with enough K, the one-pass regression arm approaches the few-step flow arm, and the flow arm needs fewer sampling steps to reach its best quality — replicating XM's jumps-versus-exploration tradeoff on a perception task; (iv) enumerating the K latents yields multi-hypothesis geometry whose spread is a calibrated, boundary-localized uncertainty. Exploration cost is modest (each candidate adds roughly a forward pass, so XM-K costs about (K+2)/3 standard steps) and is reported under matched training compute.
milestones: Literature review (Explorative Modeling and its best-of-K lineage — IMLE, multiple choice learning; the substitution between exploration and generation factoring; local-geometry evaluation and the point-gradient-matching loss from SurGe; the generative-vs-regression controlled comparison in PointDiT); stand up the shared evaluation — boundary F1, point-map normal error, AbsRel/delta1, thin-structure crops on iBims-1, ETH3D, and GSO. Kill test: on a synthetic bimodal-edge toy set (thin foreground rods over distant backgrounds), verify best-of-K training sharpens exactly what K=1 provably blurs, for both a toy regressor and a toy flow model.

Arm A — end-to-end XM on regression: train a lightweight refinement head with a latent input (Gaussian noise channel or K learned embeddings) on a frozen backbone (MoGe or Depth Anything 3) on Hypersim; sweep K in {1, 2, 3, 5, 8} with K=1 as the exact baseline; ablate the selection criterion — global pointwise loss versus edge-weighted point-gradient-matching scoring — since thin structures occupy few pixels and a global argmin dilutes their signal.

Arm B — hybrid XM on flow matching: fine-tune the released Pixel-Perfect Depth checkpoint with best-of-K exploration over input noise (same sample, timestep, and conditioning per candidate; per-sample loss selection; winner re-forwarded with gradients); sweep K at the default sampler, then sweep sampling steps (1/2/4) at fixed K to test whether exploration lets the model keep quality with fewer steps.

The head-to-head: compare both arms and their K=1 baselines under matched training compute — boundary and normal metrics at depth discontinuities, global AbsRel/delta1, NFE at inference, and qualitative point clouds of thin structures (does bent become committed-but-straight?); chart quality versus (K, sampling steps) to map the exploration-versus-factoring frontier for geometry.

(Stretch) Multi-hypothesis geometry and uncertainty: enumerate the K latents at inference for diverse plausible reconstructions of ambiguous regions, evaluating candidate spread as a boundary-localized uncertainty estimate; or per-region best-of-K selection to cover multiple independent thin structures per image.
